newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Dozens protest as Philippine court verdict nears.
newsitem.headline: Dozens protest as Philippine court verdict nears.

text.p: Leftists protested outside the Philippine Supreme Court on Tuesday hours before it was to announce the outcome of its meeting on whether to allow a petition to let President Fidel Ramos run for a second term.

A court official said the Supreme Court would issue a statement by 3.00 p.m. (0700 GMT) after its meeting to decide whether to allow a petition which wants to scrap a constitutional provision which limits a president to one six-year term.
"If they will issue one (a decision), it will be a resolution on the case," clerk of court Luzviminda Puno told Reuters.
"Otherwise, if they have no resolution to issue, I will be the one to issue a statement that there is none."

As the 15-member tribunal began its session, dozens of placard-bearing leftist workers picketed the court building to oppose any amendment to the constitution that would allow Ramos to seek re-election in the May 1998 presidential polls.
"Supreme Court rubber stamp of the Ramos regime" and "End the oppressive regime," some of the signs read.
A citizens group called PIRMA - People's Initiative for Reform, Modernisation and Action - has launched a signature collection campaign to force the calling of a referendum to amend the constitution.
PIRMA leaders said they had collected almost five million signatures so far, enough in theory to trigger a referendum on whether the 10-year-old constitution should be changed.

Analysts and politicians have warned a change could be deeply divisive in the country of 70 million which still harbours strong memories of the dictatorship under the late Ferdinand Marcos who ruled the Asian archipelago for 20 years.
The wait for a decision was unsettling the local stock market.

"Sentiment here is being affected by whether or not the Supreme Court will allow (the petition)...there's a mixed reaction and that's why we are having this sideways market," said Jose Ricardo Garcia, executive vice-president of Diversified Securities.
Some are worried that if the Court allows the petition it would show lack of stability in the country's political system, he added.
The Supreme Court decided in March that there was no law to allow constitutional amendments through petitions.
